newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - TMM's Mexico railway outlook seen optimistic.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - TMM's Mexico railway outlook seen optimistic.

text.p: Earnings estimates for the railroad recently acquired by Mexican transport company Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries Inc. are ambitious but obtainable, analysts said.

In the first year of operating the key Northwest Railway trade route, the two companies said they expect $88 million in cash flow, in the second year $358 million and in the third year $525 million, analysts were told.
"If the numbers are right they made the right business decision," said Alvaro Shiraishi, analyst with UBS Securities in New York. "That said ... even if they made a good valuation, they overpaid."

TMM and KCSI, through a partnership called Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM), won 50-year operating rights for the railroad last week with a winning bid of 11.07 billion pesos ($1.4 billion), almost three times the other two bids offered.

At a conference with analysts on Monday, the companies tried to explain the size of their investment. Company officials said they had expected key competitors Union Pacific Corp. to offer a more competitive bid with Mexican construction company partner ICA.

"If you look at Union Pacific's dependence on Mexico traffic, we're astounded their bid was just slightly over the minimum bid. It's a tremendous value creation lost by Union Pacific," KSCI president and chairman Landon Rowland said.

Union Pacific's and TFM's railroads are the only two that operate out of Laredo, Texas, serviced by the Northeast Railway. The railroad links the U.S border to Mexico City, Monterrey and key Gulf of Mexico ports.

Company officials said they plan to boost railroad use back to 1984 levels, when 20 percent of Mexico's cargo was transported by rail. Currently just 12 percent of cargo is moved over Mexico's railways, compared to 40 percent in the United States.
Rowland said the government's minimum bid for the railroad was $600 million. A spokeswoman at the Communication and Transport Ministry said it could not confirm the value of the assets.
The companies refused to discuss financing plans, although officials said at least part of financing would likely be off the companies' books.
Lack of funding details is creating some nervousness in the markets, analysts said.
"If I were a debt holder I would be more concerned than a stockholder. The question is if they can meet all the debt commitments they are required to meet," Shiraishi said.
On January 31 TFM will owe 40 percent of their bid, with the remainder due by June 5.

In the absence of funding information, Standard & Poor's and Moody's credit rating agencies put debt from the two companies on check. Caspian Securities analyst Phokion Potamianos said the brokerage downgraded TMM to market performer from buy.

"The strategy makes a lot of sense for TMM in 10 years, but I think the fears are that in the next three to four years the earnings growth will not be sufficient to maintain our forecasted growth," Potamianos said.

Planned TFM capital expenditures are $227 million for the first year, $178 million for the second year and $160 million for the third year, company officials said. These numbers include up to $90 million for equipment, and $50 million for rail improvements.

"We will be able to implement U.S.-type operation and service standards not existent in Mexico," Landon said. He said the railway will work to guarantee transit times and delivery of cars -- services not yet available in Mexico.
"Clearly they are hoping to make most of their money from labor cuts and greater operating efficiency," Potamianos said.
The companies refused to discuss labor plans, but said they will be working with unions and that "we think understand there will be adjustments."
